ce-01.title: What Civil Engineering Is
explain: **Civil engineering** is the discipline that deals with how to plan, build, and keep in service the **social infrastructure** (infrastructure) that people share, such as roads, water supply, levees, and ports. Its main object is not a house or a family home, but the foundations that a whole city or country depends on.

Social infrastructure is hard to notice in ordinary times, but its absence shows up immediately. When the water supply stops, washing and drinking become impossible; when roads are blocked, goods cannot move. It has several features:

- **Public nature**: many people share it, and it is usually the responsibility of national or local government.
- **Long lifespan**: many last for several decades, and some for more than a hundred years.
- **Large scale**: it is tied to natural features such as land, rivers, and the sea.
- **Hard to reverse once built**: so planning before construction is very important.

All four boxes are connected to the circle by lines.

explain: Civil engineering has several fields. **Structures** deal with how large structures carry loads, **geotechnics** deals with soil and foundations, **hydraulics and hydrology** deal with the flow of water, **transportation** deals with the movement of people and vehicles, and **planning and environment** deal with deciding projects and fitting them into nature. **Surveying** is the basic skill of measuring the positions and heights of land. These six lessons are an introduction that gives a taste of each of these fields.

Architecture and civil engineering overlap in some places, but their centers differ. Roughly, architecture mainly deals with buildings where people stay and the spaces inside them, while civil engineering mainly deals with the land those buildings sit on and the foundations that connect them. The boundary is blurry and differs from project to project.
The projects and figures in this course are all hypothetical, meant only to illustrate concepts. They are not standards for actual design or safety judgments.

ce-02.title: How Large Structures Stand: Beams, Arches, and Suspension
explain: A large structure such as a big bridge receives as its **load** both its own weight and the weight of the cars passing over it. The structure sends this load down through its columns and foundations into the ground. Architecture focuses on the spaces inside buildings, but here the focus is on how to cross a **long span** (the distance between supports) such as a river or a valley.

Inside materials, force appears in two main ways. A force that presses on a member is **compression**, and a force that pulls it is **tension**. Pressing a rod from above produces compression, and pulling a string from both ends produces tension.
The basic bridge types are distinguished by how they use these forces.

- **Beam bridge**: the deck itself bends and sends the load to the supports at both ends. The top of the deck is compressed and the bottom is stretched. It is the simplest type.
- **Arch bridge**: a curved arch carries the load mainly in compression and sends it down to both ends. The arch ends tend to spread outward, so solid abutments are needed.
- **Suspension bridge**: cables hung between tall towers hold up the deck in tension. The ends of the cables must be firmly anchored in the ground.

explain.alt: Three bridges stand side by side on the ground. Bridge A, a beam, has a horizontal deck resting on two columns and is labeled 'holds by bending'. Bridge B, an arch, has a horizontal deck on a semicircular arch, with outward arrows at both ends of the arch, and is labeled 'holds by pressing'. Bridge C, a suspension bridge, has a cable hanging between two towers, with vertical lines hanging from the cable that hold up the deck, and is labeled 'holds by pulling'.

explain: In general, short spans are often crossed with beams, longer ones with arch-type forms, and very long spans with suspension forms. However, this depends on ground conditions, economy, appearance, and other factors, so it is not an absolute rule.

The properties of the material also influence the choice of form. Stone and concrete are strong in compression but weak in tension, while steel cables are very strong in tension. So arches suit compression, and suspension cables suit tension.

ce-03.title: Soil and Foundations
explain: Every structure ultimately stands on the ground. However strong a structure is, if the soil beneath cannot bear it, it will tilt or sink. So in civil engineering, understanding the **ground** (the earth that supports a structure) is the starting point.

Soil is broadly divided by particle size into **gravel**, **sand**, **silt**, and **clay**, in order of decreasing particle size. Large particles let water drain through the gaps easily, while small particles let water drain slowly. Clay holds water and gradually compresses, so it can cause **settlement**, the slow sinking of a structure placed on it.

The weight of a structure is transmitted to the soil through its **foundation**. What the soil receives is not the force itself but the force per unit area, that is, **pressure**. It is the force $F$ divided by the contact area $A$.
$$p = \frac{F}{A}$$

With the same force, a larger area gives a smaller pressure. This is the same reason snowshoes keep you from sinking into snow. So a wide slab (a **footing**) is laid beneath a column to spread the load over a wider area. The unit of pressure is N/m², which is **Pa**; 1000 Pa is **kPa**. Since 1 kN = 1000 N, kN/m² is the same as kPa.

explain.alt: A flat footing labeled 2 m wide and 1 m deep sits on the ground, with a column standing on it. A downward arrow on the column is labeled 'Pressing force 600 kN'. The footing and the column rest on a layer labeled 'Soil (ground)'.
explain.caption: A wide footing spreads the column load into the soil

explain: The pressure that soil can safely bear has a limit, and that value differs greatly from one soil to another. On firm ground a shallow foundation like this is used, and where weak soil continues deep down, a **pile** (deep foundation) reaching a firm layer below is used. This lesson is only an introduction to concepts; actual foundation design requires site investigation and professional judgment based on standards.

ce-04.title: Water and Hydraulics: Understanding Discharge
explain: Civil engineering constantly meets water. Rivers, channels, drainage pipes, and dams all deal with the flow of water. The field that handles water is called **hydraulics**, and when it is viewed broadly to include the water cycle of rivers, it is also called **hydrology**.

The most basic quantity is the **discharge** (flow rate). Discharge is the volume of water passing through a cross-section divided by time, and is measured in m³/s. It is found by multiplying the cross-sectional area $A$ by the average **flow velocity** $v$.
$$Q = A \times v$$

explain.alt: A cross-section cut across a channel. The channel width is labeled 3 m and the water depth 2 m. Next to the rectangle filled with water is the label 'Flow velocity 1.5 m/s'. The label says the water flows toward the front of the figure.
explain.caption: Channel cross-section: width 3 m, depth 2 m, velocity 1.5 m/s

explain: If the cross-section is rectangular, its area is width × water depth. The channel in the figure has $A = 3 \times 2 = 6$ m² and a velocity of 1.5 m/s, so $Q = 6 \times 1.5 = 9$ m³/s. Nine cubic meters, or 9000 L, of water pass every second.

Where water neither leaks out nor is added, the discharge upstream and downstream is the same. This is called the **principle of continuity**. Therefore, when the channel narrows and its area $A$ decreases, the velocity $v$ increases to carry the same discharge. This is like water shooting out strongly when you pinch the end of a hose with your fingers.

When a river swells and its discharge suddenly increases, it becomes important whether the levee height and cross-section can accommodate it. Here only hypothetical numbers for learning the concept are dealt with; they are not criteria for actual flood preparation or river design.

ce-05.title: Roads and the Flow of Traffic
explain: A road does not end with laying the path. To think about ways to reduce congestion, you must understand how vehicles flow along it. In transportation planning, the flow of vehicles is summarized with a few quantities.

- **Traffic density** $k$: the number of vehicles per 1 km of road (vehicles/km)
- **Speed** $v$: the average speed of vehicles (km/h)
- **Traffic volume** (flow) $q$: the number of vehicles passing a point in one hour (vehicles/h)
The three quantities are related as follows.
$$q = k \times v$$

If there are 20 vehicles per km and they travel at an average of 60 km/h, then $20 \times 60 = 1200$ vehicles pass a point in one hour. One might expect that as the road fills up, the density rises and so does the traffic volume, but that is not so. When the density becomes too high, vehicles slow down greatly to avoid one another, and the traffic volume actually decreases.

explain.alt: Two long roads are drawn, each 1 km long. The upper one, A 'Light traffic road', has 5 vehicles spread apart and is labeled 80 km/h. The lower one, B 'Congested road', has 12 vehicles packed closely together and is labeled 30 km/h.
explain.caption: The same 1 km, with different densities and speeds

explain: In the figure, A gives $5 \times 80 = 400$ vehicles/h, and B gives $12 \times 30 = 360$ vehicles/h. B is much more crowded, yet fewer vehicles pass a point. This is why the number of vehicles passing actually decreases when a road is jammed.

The maximum traffic volume a road can handle is called its **capacity**. When demand approaches capacity, transportation planning compares several options, such as widening the road or using other means such as signals and public transit. The numbers in this lesson are hypothetical and are not standards for actual road planning.

ce-06.title: Project Stages, Environment, and Cost-Benefit
explain: A civil engineering project is not created all at once but goes through stages. It can roughly be divided into **planning** (what is needed), **investigation and design** (where and how), **construction** (building it), and **operation and maintenance** (managing it over a long life). Because infrastructure has a long lifespan, the last stage is the longest.

explain.alt: Four boxes are linked from left to right by arrows: 1 Planning, 2 Investigation and design, 3 Construction, 4 Operation and maintenance. Below the boxes, an orange line binds the whole, labeled 'Environmental review and public opinion recur at every stage'.
explain.caption: The four stages of a project and the review that recurs

explain: Because projects have large effects on nature, **environmental review** and **public consultation** recur at every stage. Damming a river changes the path that fish take, and building a road creates noise and cuts through forests. So during planning, alternatives and ways to reduce harm are examined together.

One method used to decide which of several plans to choose is **cost-benefit analysis**. It compares the project's **costs** (the money needed to build and manage it) and its **benefits** (the gains from the project, expressed in money). Two common indicators are these.
$$\text{Net benefit} = B - C, \qquad \text{Benefit-cost ratio} = \frac{B}{C}$$
If the benefit-cost ratio is greater than 1, benefits exceed costs. However, factors such as the change in the value of money over time (discounting) are omitted here.

Values that are hard to express in money, such as scenery, ecology, and public consensus, are difficult to capture in numbers. So cost-benefit analysis is only one ingredient in judgment and does not replace the conclusion. All projects and figures in this lesson are hypothetical.

examples.title: Two hypothetical projects
body: In a hypothetical county, two projects are compared. Project A has total benefits of 120 eok won (1 eok won = 100 million won) and total costs of 80 eok won. Its net benefit is $120 - 80 = 40$ eok won, and its benefit-cost ratio is $120 / 80 = 1.5$. Project B has total benefits of 90 eok won and total costs of 100 eok won, so its net benefit is $-10$ eok won and its benefit-cost ratio is 0.9. Looking at the numbers alone, Project A is better.

ce-07.title: Reactions of Statically Determinate Beams and Equilibrium Equations
explain: In stage 1 we learned that a bridge sends its load through its supports into the ground. But how much force does a single support actually bear? We need this value to decide the sizes of supports, piers, and foundations. The force that a support pushes back on a structure to hold it up is called a **reaction**, and finding the reactions is the first step of structural analysis.

The starting point is the **equilibrium** condition of statics. The sum of all forces and of all moments (the turning effect, force × perpendicular distance to the center of rotation) acting on a body that does not move must be zero. For a planar structure there are three equations: $$\sum F_x = 0, \quad \sum F_y = 0, \quad \sum M = 0$$ A diagram in which the structure is detached from its supports and all loads and reactions are drawn as arrows is called a **free body diagram**. Equilibrium equations are always written on the free body diagram.

The number of reactions a support produces depends on which movements it prevents. A **pin (hinge)** prevents horizontal and vertical movement, giving 2 reactions. A **roller** prevents only movement perpendicular to its support surface, giving 1 reaction. A **fixed end** prevents both movement and rotation, giving 2 reactions and 1 moment, for 3 in total. When the number of unknown reactions equals the number of equilibrium equations (3), so that the structure can be solved by equilibrium alone, it is called a **statically determinate** structure. When there are more unknowns, requiring deformation conditions as well, it is a **statically indeterminate** structure. A **simply supported beam**, with a pin on one end and a roller on the other, is a typical determinate beam.

Let us derive the reactions of a simply supported beam. For a beam of length $L$, at a distance $a$ from A there is a load $P$, and let $b = L - a$ be the distance from the load to B. Setting the sum of moments about A to zero gives $R_B \cdot L - P \cdot a = 0$, that is, $R_B = Pa/L$. From the sum of vertical forces, $R_A = P - R_B = Pb/L$. The support closer to the load receives the larger reaction. For a uniformly distributed load $w$ (load per unit length), treat the resultant $wL$ as acting at the middle of the span and use the same method.

The dimension line below shows "2 m", "4 m", and the total "L = 6 m", and above the beam is written "Simply supported beam (self-weight of the beam ignored)".

explain: Let us read the figure. $L = 6$ m, and the load $P = 30$ kN is 2 m from A and 4 m from B. From the moment equilibrium about A, $R_B = 30 \times 2 / 6 = 10$ kN, and $R_A = 30 - 10 = 20$ kN. As a check, taking moments about B gives $R_A \times 6 = 30 \times 4$, so the same values result. With no horizontal load, the horizontal reaction at the pin is zero.

Limits and exceptions: this calculation rests on the assumption that the beam is in equilibrium as a rigid body. In statically indeterminate structures, such as a beam fixed at both ends or a continuous beam with three or more supports, the reactions are not determined by the equilibrium equations alone; the deflection of the beam and the stiffness of the material must also be considered. In addition, actual bridge loads are set by combining several cases such as vehicle positions, wind, temperature, and earthquakes. The numbers in this lesson are hypothetical values for practicing the concepts.

ce-08.title: Shear Force, Bending Moment, and Bending Stress
explain: Knowing the reactions does not tell us whether a beam is safe. A beam actually fails not at its supports but inside its body. To determine the size of the cross-section and the material, we must know how much force acts at each cross-section within the beam. The internal forces that arise inside a beam are called **section forces**.

If we imaginarily cut the beam at one location and draw a free body diagram of only the left piece, the cut face must carry two kinds of internal force for the left piece to be in equilibrium: the **shear force** $V$, which tends to slide the two sides of the section up and down relative to each other, and the **bending moment** $M$, which bends the section. In a simply supported beam, the moment that causes sagging (stretching the bottom) is usually taken as positive.

The procedure is as follows. ① Find the reactions. ② Divide the beam into segments at each point where the load changes. ③ In each segment, cut the beam and write $V$ and $M$ as equations. ④ The graphs drawn from these are the **shear force diagram** (SFD) and the **bending moment diagram** (BMD). The two graphs are related by $\frac{dM}{dx} = V$, so the moment is largest where the shear force becomes zero (changes sign). For a simply supported beam with a concentrated load, the maximum moment is $M_{max} = Pab/L$ under the load; for a simply supported beam with a uniformly distributed load, it is $M_{max} = wL^2/8$ at midspan.

explain.alt: Diagram of a simply supported beam. The left support A is a triangular support (pin), and the right support B is a support with two wheels (roller). At 2 m to the right of A there is a downward arrow labeled "P = 30 kN". Below both supports are upward arrows R_A and R_B. The dimension line below shows "2 m", "4 m", and the total "L = 6 m", and above the beam is written "Simply supported beam (self-weight of the beam ignored)".

explain: Let us read the beam in the figure. The reactions are $R_A = 20$ kN and $R_B = 10$ kN. From A to the load point the shear force is +20 kN, and after passing the load point it becomes $20 - 30 = -10$ kN, changing sign. Therefore the maximum moment occurs under the load, and from the equilibrium of the left piece, $M = 20 \times 2 = 40$ kN·m. The formula $Pab/L = 30 \times 2 \times 4 / 6$ gives the same value.

The stress that a moment produces in the cross-section is the **bending stress**. Assuming the cross-section remains plane within the linear elastic range, $\sigma = My/I$, which is zero at the neutral axis and largest at the top and bottom edges. The edge stress is written $\sigma_{max} = M/S$, where $S$ is the **section modulus**. For a rectangle of width $b$ and height $h$, $S = bh^2/6$, which is proportional to the square of the height. This is why the same board carries far more load when set on edge than when laid flat.

Limits and exceptions: $\sigma = M/S$ holds for beams whose height is small relative to their length, within the elastic range, and under the plane-section assumption. Deep beams whose height approaches the span, behavior after the material yields, and materials such as concrete whose tension side cracks require different models (next lesson). Failure by shear and limits on deflection must also be checked separately, and this lesson is not a design standard.

ce-09.title: Buckling of Columns, Reinforced and Prestressed Concrete
explain: A member that receives a compressive force can bend sideways before the material is crushed. Pressing a thin ruler from both ends makes it bow like a bow before it breaks. The sudden sideways bending in which a compression member loses its ability to carry load is called **buckling**. Buckling depends strongly on the length and cross-sectional shape of the member, regardless of the strength of the material.

Euler derived the **critical load** at which an ideal, straight, elastic column begins to bend. $$P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 E I}{(KL)^2}$$ Here $E$ is the modulus of elasticity, $I$ is the second moment of area (how hard the section is to bend), $L$ is the length, and $K$ is the **effective length factor** that depends on the support conditions. The theoretical values are 1.0 for pinned at both ends, 0.5 for fixed at both ends, 2.0 for fixed at one end and free at the other, and about 0.7 for fixed at one end and pinned at the other. Because the critical load is inversely proportional to $(KL)^2$, doubling the length reduces it to one quarter.

Now let us turn to materials. Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, with a tensile strength of roughly one tenth of its compressive strength. In a simply supported beam the bottom is pulled, so a beam made of concrete alone cracks and fails easily starting from the bottom. Therefore **steel reinforcing bars** are placed on the tension side to carry the pulling force. This is **reinforced concrete** (RC).

The flexural strength of an RC beam is derived as a force couple formed by the two forces in the section. When the reinforcement yields, the tensile force is $T = A_s f_y$ ($A_s$ is the area of the reinforcement and $f_y$ its yield strength). Approximating the compressed concrete at the top by a rectangular block of depth $a$, the compressive force is $C = 0.85 f_{ck} a b$ ($f_{ck}$ is the compressive strength of the concrete and $b$ the width). Setting $C = T$ gives $a = A_s f_y / (0.85 f_{ck} b)$. The distance between the two forces is $d - a/2$ ($d$ is the effective depth from the compression face to the centroid of the reinforcement), so the nominal flexural strength is $M_n = A_s f_y (d - a/2)$.

**Prestressed concrete** (PSC) goes one step further: high-strength steel tendons are pulled in advance to put compression into the concrete. If the tendons are placed below the center of the section (eccentrically), the compression introduced in advance cancels the tension that the load would create at the bottom, reducing or eliminating cracks at service loads. It can span longer distances at the same depth and is widely used in bridge girders.

Limits and exceptions: Euler's formula is the ideal value for slender, straight, elastic columns. Short, thick columns have their material yield before buckling, and real columns are initially slightly bent or have loads off center, so problems arise at loads smaller than the critical load. The RC strength formula also rests on the assumption that the reinforcement yields first. Actual design follows standards that use strength reduction factors and load factors, and the numbers in this lesson are hypothetical.

ce-10.title: Three-Phase Relations of Soil and Compaction
explain: Even the same sand behaves quite differently when it is compacted tightly versus when it is loose. Its weight and strength also change with how much water it holds. To handle soil with numbers, we must first divide what a lump of soil is made of.

Soil consists of three phases: **soil particles** (solid), and **water** and **air** filling the **voids** (gaps between the particles). Drawing these together gives the **three-phase diagram**. Letting $V_s$ be the volume of the particles, $V_w$ the volume of water, $V_a$ the volume of air, and the void volume $V_v = V_w + V_a$, the main indices are as follows.

- **Void ratio** $e = V_v / V_s$: the ratio of void volume to particle volume
- **Porosity** $n = V_v / V$: the ratio of voids to total volume, $n = e/(1+e)$
- **Water content** $w = W_w / W_s$: the ratio of water weight to particle weight (as a percentage)
- **Degree of saturation** $S = V_w / V_v$: the fraction of the voids filled with water
- **Specific gravity** $G_s$: the particle density divided by the density of water (usually 2.6 to 2.8)

These indices are related to one another. Taking the particle volume as 1, the void volume is $e$ and the water volume is $Se$. Dividing the water weight $Se\gamma_w$ by the particle weight $G_s\gamma_w$ gives $w$, which leads to the basic relation $$Se = wG_s$$. In the same way, the unit weight is $\gamma = \frac{(G_s + Se)\gamma_w}{1+e}$ and the dry unit weight is $\gamma_d = \frac{G_s \gamma_w}{1+e} = \frac{\gamma}{1+w}$.

explain.alt: Three-phase diagram of 1.0 m³ of soil. Three boxes are stacked vertically. The top box is labeled "Air" 0.1 m³, the middle box "Water" 0.3 m³, and the bottom box "Soil particles" 0.6 m³. A bracket tying the air and water boxes together is labeled "Voids", and below the diagram is written "Total 1.0 m³". In the lower left it is written "Volume (sizes approximate)".

explain: Reading the figure, $V_s = 0.6$, $V_w = 0.3$, and $V_a = 0.1$ m³. The void volume is 0.4 m³, so $e = 0.4/0.6 \approx 0.67$ and $n = 0.4/1.0 = 0.4$. The degree of saturation is read as the fraction of the voids that is filled with water.

The representative operation that uses these relations is **compaction**: tapping or pressing soil to drive out air and raise the dry unit weight. When soil is compacted with the same compaction energy while its water content is varied, the dry unit weight first rises and then, beyond a certain water content, falls. The water content at the peak is the **optimum water content**, and the value there is the **maximum dry unit weight**. With too little water, particles do not slide easily past one another; with too much, water occupies the voids and keeps the particles from coming closer. Compaction control standards differ by test method and project, and this lesson covers only the concept.

ce-11.title: Terzaghi Effective Stress and Consolidation Settlement
explain: At a point inside soil, the weight of the soil and water above presses down. However, the soil skeleton does not carry all of this weight. The water that fills the voids shares the pressure as well. Which of the two governs the strength and deformation of soil? Terzaghi's answer to this question is the **principle of effective stress**.

The **total stress** $\sigma$ at a point is the sum of the unit weight times the thickness of the soil above it, $\sigma = \sum \gamma_i h_i$. The **pore water pressure** at that point, at a depth $h_w$ below the water table, is $u = \gamma_w h_w$. The force carried by contact between soil particles is the difference between the two. $$\sigma' = \sigma - u$$ This $\sigma'$ is called the **effective stress**, and the compression and shear strength of soil are governed by the effective stress.

explain.alt: Cross-section of the ground. From the surface down to a depth of 3 m is a layer labeled "Sand γ = 18 kN/m³". At a depth of 3 m, a dashed line and an inverted triangle mark the "Groundwater level". Below that, a 4 m thick layer is labeled "Clay (saturated) γsat = 20 kN/m³", and below that is a "Firm layer". At the bottom of the clay layer an orange dot A is marked. On the right, the dimension lines are labeled "3 m" and "4 m", and below is written "Unit weight of water γw = 9.81 kN/m³".

explain: Let us calculate point A in the figure. The total stress is the sum of the sand layer $18 \times 3$ and the clay layer $20 \times 4$, and the pore water pressure is the unit weight of water times the depth of 4 m below the groundwater level. Note that when the groundwater level rises or falls, the pore water pressure changes, and so does the effective stress at the same depth.

**Consolidation** is the process in which changes in effective stress take place over time. When soil is placed on saturated clay, at first the water bears most of the added load, creating **excess pore water pressure**. Clay has very low permeability, so the water drains out slowly, and as it drains the load is transferred to the soil skeleton, increasing the effective stress and compressing the soil. So settlement of clay ground proceeds over months to years.

For normally consolidated clay, the final settlement is often estimated with the compression index $C_c$ as follows. $$S_c = \frac{C_c H}{1+e_0} \log_{10} \frac{\sigma'_0 + \Delta\sigma}{\sigma'_0}$$ Here $H$ is the layer thickness, $e_0$ is the initial void ratio, $\sigma'_0$ is the initial effective stress, and $\Delta\sigma$ is the increase in stress. The time for settlement is estimated as $t = T_v H_{dr}^2 / c_v$, where $H_{dr}$ is the maximum drainage distance, which is half the layer thickness when drainage occurs on both sides. The time factor corresponding to 50% average degree of consolidation is about 0.197.

Limits and exceptions: this formula assumes normal consolidation, one-dimensional deformation (no lateral spreading), and a homogeneous layer. Overconsolidated clay, which has previously been loaded more heavily, uses a different index, and there is secondary compression that proceeds slowly even after consolidation ends. The coefficients for real ground are determined from sample tests and field measurements, and the values in this lesson are hypothetical.

Step 2: $\log_{10}(200/100) \approx 0.301$, so $S_c \approx 0.6 \times 0.301 \approx 0.18$ m.
Interpretation: even though the stress doubles, the settlement grows logarithmically. For the same increase, it appears larger in a shallow layer where the initial effective stress is small.

Step 2: $t_{50} = 0.197 \times 2^2 / 2 \approx 0.39$ year, about five months.

Interpretation: time is proportional to the square of the drainage distance. If drainage occurs on one side only, $H_{dr} = 4$ m and the time quadruples. This is why methods that shorten the drainage distance are used.

ce-12.title: Mohr-Coulomb Shear Strength and Bearing Capacity
explain: A slope collapsing, or soil beneath a foundation being pushed out sideways, are all **shear failure**, in which the soil slides along some surface. Soil is not a single mass like concrete but an assembly of particles, so what determines its strength is the friction and interlocking between the particles. Then what determines the maximum shear stress that soil can withstand?

Coulomb applied the principle of friction to soil and concluded that the greater the force pressing on a surface, the harder it is to slide. As discussed in the previous lesson, the behavior of soil is governed by effective stress, so the **shear strength** on the failure surface is as follows. $$\tau_f = c' + \sigma' \tan\phi'$$ $c'$ is the **cohesion** (the strength present even without any pressing force), and $\phi'$ is the **internal friction angle**. Clean sand has $c'$ close to zero, while clay shows a cohesive component depending on conditions.

The stress state at a point in soil is represented by a **Mohr circle**: a circle whose diameter runs between the major principal stress $\sigma_1$ and the minor principal stress $\sigma_3$. When the circle touches the upper straight line (the **failure envelope**), the point fails. For soil with $c' = 0$, the condition at which the circle touches the line gives $\sin\phi' = \frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{\sigma_1 + \sigma_3}$, and the failure plane makes an angle of $45^{\circ} + \phi'/2$ with the plane of the major principal stress. The triaxial test uses this relation to find $\phi'$.

explain.alt: Graph. The horizontal axis is effective normal stress σ' (kPa) with ticks at 0, 50, 100, 150, and 200, and the vertical axis is shear stress τ (kPa) with ticks at 0, 40, 80, and 120. At 20 on the vertical axis an orange dot is marked with "c' = 20 kPa", and from that point a straight green line runs up and to the right, labeled "Failure envelope (φ' = 30°)". Below it is written "Above the line: failure / below the line: stable".

explain: Reading the graph, the line starts at 20 kPa on the vertical axis and has slope $\tan 30^{\circ} \approx 0.577$. The shear strength on a plane with effective normal stress 100 kPa is $20 + 100 \times 0.577 \approx 77.7$ kPa. If the stress point lies below the line, that plane is stable; if it reaches the line, it fails.

Shear strength leads to the **bearing capacity** of a foundation. As the load on the foundation keeps increasing, the soil beneath is pushed out along a sliding surface, and the pressure just before this happens is the **ultimate bearing capacity** $q_u$. For a continuous (strip) foundation, the form proposed by Terzaghi is $$q_u = cN_c + qN_q + \frac{1}{2}\gamma B N_\gamma$$ Here $q = \gamma D_f$ is the weight of soil down to the foundation depth, $B$ is the width of the foundation, and $N_c, N_q, N_\gamma$ are the **bearing capacity factors**, which increase with $\phi'$. The values of these factors differ somewhat among proposers and methods, so this course uses the values given in each problem. Dividing the ultimate value by a factor of safety (typically about 3) gives the **allowable bearing capacity**.

Limits and exceptions: a straight failure envelope may curve over a wide stress range. When a load is applied quickly to saturated clay and there is no time for water to drain, it is treated separately as the undrained strength. When loose saturated sand is shaken by an earthquake, pore water pressure can rise sharply and the effective stress approaches zero, which is called **liquefaction**. The bearing capacity formula is a conceptual formula that assumes homogeneous ground and simple loading, and actual judgment follows investigation and standards.

ce-13.title: Continuity and Energy Equations
explain: A water supply pipe carries water from a high reservoir down to a low town. Where the pipe narrows, how much faster does the water flow, and what happens to the pressure? The $Q = Av$ learned in stage 1 tells us the flow rate, but it does not tell us the relation between pressure and height. The two equations that handle this are the **continuity equation** and the **energy equation**.

The **continuity equation** expresses conservation of mass. If water is treated as an incompressible fluid, the discharge through any cross-section of a pipe with no leaks is the same. $$Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$ Since the cross-sectional area of a circular pipe is $A = \pi D^2/4$, halving the diameter reduces the area to one quarter and increases the velocity fourfold.

The **energy equation** expresses conservation of energy. The energy per unit weight of water, expressed in units of length, is called **head**, and there are three kinds: the **elevation head** $z$, which is the height itself; the **pressure head** $p/\gamma$, which is the height to which the pressure can push the water up; and the **velocity head** $v^2/2g$, which is the energy of the velocity. Along a streamline where friction can be neglected, the sum of these is constant; this is the **Bernoulli equation**. $$z_1 + \frac{p_1}{\gamma} + \frac{v_1^2}{2g} = z_2 + \frac{p_2}{\gamma} + \frac{v_2^2}{2g}$$ In a real pipe, the head loss $h_L$ is added to the right-hand side.

Viewed as steps, the derivation goes as follows. ① Choose two cross-sections. ② Use the continuity equation to find the velocity at each section. ③ Insert the elevation, pressure, and velocity heads into the energy equation. ④ Find the remaining unknown, usually a pressure or a water level. In a horizontal pipe that narrows, $z$ is the same and the velocity head grows, so the pressure head falls by the same amount. A Venturi meter uses this pressure difference to measure the flow rate.

As a special case, consider water emerging from a small hole in the side of a large tank. The free surface and the hole are both at atmospheric pressure, and the surface velocity is nearly zero, so the whole height $h$ from the surface to the hole converts into velocity head. This gives $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, which is called **Torricelli's theorem**. It is the same speed as an object dropped from a height $h$.

Limits and exceptions: the Bernoulli equation holds under the assumptions of steady flow, incompressibility, no friction, and a single streamline. In long pipes the friction loss is large (next lesson), and in sections where a pump adds energy or a turbine removes it, that energy must be included in the equation. Also, using the mean velocity over a cross-section creates a difference from the actual velocity distribution.

ce-14.title: Friction Loss in Pressurized Pipes
explain: According to the Bernoulli equation from the previous lesson, water in a high reservoir should flow to a low reservoir ever faster without limit. In reality, friction with the pipe wall and eddies within the water convert energy into heat and slow the flow. When designing a long water main, one must know this **head loss** in order to choose a pipe diameter that delivers the desired flow rate.

Friction loss in pipes is expressed by the **Darcy-Weisbach equation**. $$h_f = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{v^2}{2g}$$ The loss is proportional to the pipe length $L$, inversely proportional to the diameter $D$, and proportional to the velocity head. $f$ is the **friction factor**, which depends on the flow regime and the roughness of the pipe wall.

The flow regime is separated by the **Reynolds number** $Re = vD/\nu$ ($\nu$ is the kinematic viscosity). In a circular pipe, roughly $Re < 2000$ is **laminar flow**, in which water slides in layers, and there $f = 64/Re$ is derived exactly. Above about 4000 is **turbulent flow**, in which eddies mix the water, and $f$ is read from the experimentally obtained Moody diagram or from approximations, depending on $Re$ and the relative roughness. Flow in water supply pipes is mostly turbulent. **Minor losses** at valves, bends, and entrances are added separately as $h_m = K v^2/2g$.

explain.alt: Diagram of a pipe connecting two reservoirs. The water surface of the left "Reservoir A" is labeled "Water surface 50 m", and the water surface of the right "Reservoir B" is labeled "Water surface 38 m". A horizontal pipe connects the lower parts of the two reservoirs, and an orange dotted line descending from the water surface of A to the water surface of B is labeled "Energy line". Below it is written "Pipe: L = 1000 m, D = 0.3 m, f = 0.02" and "Minor losses (entrance and exit) ignored".

explain: Let us solve the two-reservoir problem in the figure step by step. ① Write the energy equation between the two water surfaces. Both are at atmospheric pressure and the surface velocities are nearly zero, so the whole difference in water level becomes loss. ② If minor losses are ignored, $h_f = 50 - 38$. ③ Insert $f$, $L$, and $D$ into the Darcy-Weisbach equation to find $v$. ④ Find the flow rate with $Q = \pi D^2 / 4 \times v$. The energy line slopes steadily down from A to B by exactly this loss.

Limits and exceptions: for turbulent flow, $f$ changes slightly with velocity, so in practice one assumes $f$, computes, and repeats the calculation (iteration). As a pipe ages, its wall becomes rougher and $f$ increases. In a short pipeline with many fittings, the minor losses can be larger than the friction loss. In practice the empirical Hazen-Williams equation is also used, but its range is limited to water and certain conditions.

ce-15.title: Manning's Formula for Open Channels and Peak Runoff by the Rational Method
explain: A drainage ditch or river in a city is an **open channel**, flowing under gravity with its top open. To keep the channel from overflowing when it rains, two things must be known: the flow the channel can pass (**conveyance capacity**) and the flow that enters the channel from rainfall (**runoff**). Hydraulics handles the former, and hydrology handles the latter.

In steady uniform flow in an open channel (**uniform flow**), the gravity component from the channel slope and the wall friction are in balance. The empirical relation that summarizes this balance is the **Manning equation**. $$v = \frac{1}{n} R^{2/3} S^{1/2}$$ Here $n$ is the **roughness coefficient** of the wall (small for smooth concrete, large for natural channels with grass and rocks), $S$ is the channel bed slope, and $R = A/P$ is the **hydraulic radius**, the flow cross-sectional area $A$ divided by the wetted perimeter $P$. SI units (m and s) are used.

For a rectangular channel with bed width $b$ and water depth $y$, $A = by$ and $P = b + 2y$, since the water surface is not included in the wetted perimeter. The conveyance capacity is $Q = Av$. Even with the same area, a shorter wetted perimeter gives a larger $R$, so the water flows more easily.

On the runoff side, the classic method for estimating the **peak discharge** (the largest discharge) of a small watershed is the **rational method**. $$Q = \frac{1}{3.6} C I A$$ Here $Q$ is in m³/s, $C$ is the **runoff coefficient** (the fraction of rain that runs off rather than soaking into the ground; large for paved surfaces and small for vegetated areas), $I$ is the **rainfall intensity** (mm/h), and $A$ is the watershed area (km²). The factor 3.6 makes the units consistent. The rainfall intensity used is that of rain lasting for the **time of concentration**, the time for water from the farthest point of the watershed to reach the outlet. If the watershed has mixed land types, $C$ is taken as an area-weighted average.

Connecting the two formulas shows the framework of drainage planning. The rational method gives the flow that will enter the channel, Manning's formula gives the conveyance capacity of the channel, and the two are compared. When urbanization paves green land, $C$ increases; water gathers quickly along smooth roads and pipes, so the time of concentration shortens and a stronger short-duration rainfall intensity is used. The peak runoff therefore increases together.

Limits and exceptions: the rational method assumes that rain falls evenly over the whole catchment and that its intensity is constant over the time of concentration. It is therefore used mainly for small catchments; for large catchments, methods such as unit hydrographs, which describe runoff over time, are used. Manning's formula assumes uniform flow, and the result depends greatly on the choice of $n$. The numbers in this lesson are hypothetical and are not standards for actual flood preparation.

ce-16.title: Construction Management: Schedules and the Critical Path
explain: Completing a design does not by itself produce a facility. Dozens of tasks must be arranged in what order, and when each should start and finish. Some tasks cannot start until a preceding task is complete, while others may proceed at the same time. A **schedule** determines the total construction period (**duration**) and identifies the tasks that must not be delayed.

First divide the work into manageable tasks (work breakdown), and determine the duration of each task and its **precedence relations**. Drawing the tasks as boxes and the precedence relations as arrows gives a **network schedule**. Among the paths from start to finish through the network, the path with the greatest sum of durations is the **critical path**, and its length is the minimum duration. This method is called **CPM**.

The calculation runs in two directions. **Forward pass**: the earliest start (ES) of each task is the maximum of the earliest finishes (EF) of its preceding tasks, and $EF = ES + $ duration. **Backward pass**: starting from the latest finish (LF) of the last task, set equal to the total duration, move backward; the latest start is $LS = LF - $ duration, and the LF of a preceding task is the minimum of the LS of the tasks that follow it. The **total float** of a task is $LS - ES$, and the tasks with zero float form the critical path.

explain.alt: Diagram of a task network. Arrows run from "Start" to "A Excavation 4 days" and to "C Materials delivery 2 days". From A, arrows run to "B Foundation pouring 3 days" and to "E Drainage pipe 3 days". Arrows from B and C enter "D Wall construction 5 days". Arrows from D and E enter "F Backfilling 2 days". Below it is written "Arrow: the next task starts only after the preceding task ends".

explain: Let us read the network in the figure. There are three paths: A-B-D-F, A-E-F, and C-D-F. Adding the durations of each path and finding the longest gives the critical path and the duration. If a task on the critical path is delayed by one day, the whole duration is delayed by one day, but a task with float may be delayed by as much as its float without affecting the duration.

When the duration must be shortened, the tasks on the critical path must be shortened (**schedule compression**). Shortening a task that is not on the critical path has no effect. Also, if a critical-path task is shortened too much, another path becomes the new critical path, so the paths must be checked again at each reduction. Compression usually costs extra equipment or labor, so the critical-path tasks with the lowest cost of compression are shortened first.

Limits and exceptions: CPM assumes that task durations are fixed. Actual durations fluctuate with weather, ground conditions, and material supply, so methods that treat durations as probabilities (such as PERT) are also used. In addition, if equipment and labor are limited, even a task with float may be unable to proceed at the same time as others because of resource constraints. This lesson covers only the concepts of schedule calculation and is not guidance on site work methods or safety procedures.

examples.title: Critical path of a small network
body: Condition: P (3 days) is followed by Q (4 days) and R (6 days), and S (2 days) can start only after both Q and R are complete.
Step 1 (paths): P-Q-S is $3 + 4 + 2 = 9$ days, and P-R-S is $3 + 6 + 2 = 11$ days.
Step 2: the critical path is P-R-S, with a duration of 11 days. The total float of Q is $11 - 9 = 2$ days.
Interpretation: even if Q is delayed by up to 2 days, the duration stays the same; if it is delayed by 3 days, the duration increases by one day.

body: Condition: in the network above, we want to reduce the duration.

Step 2: shortening the critical task R by 3 days makes P-R-S 8 days, but P-Q-S is 9 days, so the duration becomes 9 days and the critical path changes to P-Q-S.
Interpretation: the effect of compression stops at the second-longest path. Therefore compression proceeds one step at a time, rechecking the paths each time.

ce-17.title: Load Transfer Systems of Bridges and Tunnels
explain: Bridges and tunnels solve opposite problems. A bridge floats a road over empty space, while a tunnel creates an empty space within solid ground. Both begin with understanding the path along which loads reach the ground, that is, the **load path**.

A bridge is roughly divided into three parts. The **superstructure** consists of the **deck**, which vehicles directly contact, and the **girders** (main beams) that support it. The **bearings** support the superstructure. The **substructure** consists of the **abutments** (at the ends) and **piers** (in the middle), together with the **foundations** beneath them. Vehicle loads flow in the order deck, girders, bearings, piers and abutments, foundations, ground. The reactions and moments learned in stage 2 are the tools for checking the girders, and the bearing capacity from stage 3 is the tool for checking the foundations.

**Bearings** transmit loads while allowing the superstructure to expand and contract with temperature. When a member of length $L$ undergoes a temperature change $\Delta T$, its length changes by $$\Delta L = \alpha L \Delta T$$ $\alpha$ is the **coefficient of thermal expansion**; it is about $1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ /^{\circ}C for steel and about $1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ /°C for concrete. To accommodate this movement, an **expansion joint** is placed at the end of the bridge. If the expansion is prevented, a correspondingly large axial force develops in the member and in the bearings.

The commonly used forms also change with the span length. Short spans are often girder bridges, longer spans are arches or trusses, and very long spans are often cable-stayed or suspension bridges. However, this is only a tendency; the choice depends on terrain, ground, cost, appearance, and construction conditions.

When a tunnel is excavated, the load of the soil and rock that was supported at that location loses its support and is **redistributed** to the surroundings of the excavation face. If an **arching effect** develops, in which the surrounding ground carries the load around the opening like an arch, the load on the support is reduced. Therefore, in sound rock tunnels, concepts such as shotcrete (sprayed concrete) and rock bolts are used to help the ground itself act as support. In soft ground or beneath urban areas, a shield TBM method is sometimes used, which excavates inside a cylindrical steel shell while the lining is assembled immediately. When groundwater is abundant, whether to drain it or block it is also a major decision.

Limits and exceptions: this lesson introduces the concepts of forms and load paths; it is not guidance on construction procedures or safety standards. Actual bridges and tunnels examine many conditions together, such as earthquakes, wind, fatigue, and scour (the erosion of soil around foundations by flowing water).

examples.title: Thermal expansion of a steel bridge
body: Condition: a steel girder 100 m long, with a temperature change of 50 °C over the year and $\alpha = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ /°C.
Step 1: $\Delta L = 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 100 \times 50$.
Step 2: $\Delta L = 0.06$ m, that is, 60 mm.
Interpretation: the expansion joints and movable bearings must accommodate movement of this size. The longer the girder, the larger the joint must be.

examples.title: Following the load path
body: Condition: one truck on a hypothetical three-span girder bridge.
Step 1: the wheel load passes through the deck and is divided among the nearby girders.
Step 2: the girders carry this load by bending to the bearings at both ends, and the bearings pass it through the piers to the foundations and the ground.
Interpretation: if any single element along the path fails to carry its load, the whole structure is at risk. Therefore the check covers every element of the path.

checks.prompt: List in order the sequence in which the vehicle load is transferred to the ground in a girder bridge.
checks.hint: Follow it from top to bottom, from the place the vehicle touches down to the ground.
checks.explanation: Superstructure, then bearing, then substructure, then foundation, then ground.

checks.prompt: A 60 m concrete bridge deck undergoes a temperature change from −10 °C in winter to 40 °C in summer. With $\alpha = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ /°C, what is the change in length? (mm)
checks.hint: First find the temperature change, then convert m to mm.
checks.explanation: $\Delta T = 50$ °C, so $\Delta L = 10^{-5} \times 60 \times 50 = 0.03$ m = 30 mm.

checks.prompt: Which statement about the ground around a tunnel after excavation is correct?
checks.hint: If the load loses its path, think about where it can go.
checks.explanation: Stress redistribution and the arching effect are the basis of the tunnel support concept.
options: All the load above the excavated space disappears
The load is redistributed to the surroundings of the excavation face, and the ground can carry load around it like an arch
The stress in the ground is exactly the same as before excavation
Groundwater is unrelated to the stability of the tunnel

checks.prompt: The two ends of a long steel bridge are fully fixed so that they cannot move, with no expansion joint. In summer the temperature rises greatly. What is most likely to happen?
checks.hint: If an expansion that should occur is blocked, a force takes its place.
checks.explanation: Blocked thermal expansion appears as thermal stress, that is, a large internal axial force.
options: The girder expands freely, so no force develops
The girder becomes shorter
The coefficient of thermal expansion becomes zero
Because the expansion is blocked, large compressive forces develop in the girder and bearings

ce-18.title: Lifecycle Maintenance of Social Infrastructure
explain: Infrastructure is used for several decades after it is built. During that time, concrete cracks, reinforcement rusts, and traffic volume and climate change. If the timing of inspection, repair, and replacement is decided poorly, costs rise greatly or safety is threatened. The perspective that manages a facility across its whole life is called **lifecycle management**.

The foundation of management is **inspection**. Inspection is divided by depth: routine inspection, in which abnormal signs are watched often by eye; periodic inspection at set intervals; and detailed inspection and diagnosis, which evaluate the causes and performance in detail with equipment and tests. Inspection results are often summarized as several levels of **condition grade** or as a **condition index** from 0 to 100. Measures can be divided into **repair**, which fixes damage to restore the original function; **reinforcement**, which raises the load-carrying capacity beyond the original; and **replacement**.

The condition of a facility declines over time, tending to decline slowly at first and faster as damage accumulates. The graph of this is the **deterioration curve**. Rather than **reactive repair** after the condition has become very poor, **preventive maintenance**, which acts while the condition is still good at a small cost, often extends the service life and reduces the total cost.

explain.alt: Graph. The horizontal axis is elapsed years from 0 to 50, and the vertical axis is condition index from 0 to 100. A gray dashed line "Repair threshold 50" is at a condition index of 50. An orange dashed line "Curve 1: no repair" connects 0 years at 100, 10 years at 90, 20 years at 75, 30 years at 50, and 40 years at 20. A solid green line "Curve 2: preventive repair at year 15" follows curve 1 until year 15, jumps to 95 at year 15, and connects 25 years at 85, 35 years at 70, 45 years at 50, and 50 years at 38.

explain: Let us read the graph. Curve 1 falls without repair and reaches the repair threshold of 50. Curve 2 raises the condition index with preventive repair at year 15 and then falls more slowly. The difference between the years when the two curves reach the threshold is the period gained by preventive repair. Whether the value of that period exceeds the cost of the preventive repair is the next question to examine.

A tool for comparing management alternatives is the **life-cycle cost** (LCC) analysis. It adds the initial construction cost and all future costs of maintenance, repair, replacement, and demolition. Because money in the future has a different value from money today, future amounts are converted to present value using a **discount rate** $i$. The present value of a cost incurred after $t$ years, with amount $F$, is $$PV = \frac{F}{(1+i)^t}$$ The higher the discount rate, the smaller the present value of costs in the distant future.

Limits and exceptions: a deterioration curve is an average tendency obtained from data on facilities of the same type, so it may differ from the actual condition of an individual facility. Because the ranking of alternatives can change with the discount rate chosen, it is common to also check how much the results shift across several discount rates (sensitivity). Values that are hard to convert into money, such as safety and user benefits, are considered separately. The projects and numbers in this lesson are all hypothetical.

examples.title: Lifecycle cost of two management plans
body: Condition: Plan A has an initial cost of 100 eok won (1 eok won = 100 million won) and a repair cost of 60 eok won 20 years later. Plan B has an initial cost of 120 eok won and a repair cost of 20 eok won 20 years later. Discount rate 4%, $(1.04)^{20} \approx 2.191$.
Step 1 (without discounting): A totals 160 eok won and B totals 140 eok won, so B appears cheaper.
Step 2 (with discounting): A is $100 + 60/2.191 \approx 127.4$ eok won and B is $120 + 20/2.191 \approx 129.1$ eok won, so A is slightly cheaper.
Interpretation: the ranking reversed depending on whether discounting is applied. When the difference is small, the discount rate assumption and non-monetary values must be examined together.

examples.title: Reading the period gained by preventive repair
body: Condition: the two curves in the graph above and the repair threshold of 50.
Step 1: read from the horizontal axis the year in which curve 1 reaches the threshold.
Step 2: read in the same way the year in which curve 2 reaches the threshold, and find the difference between the two.

Interpretation: comparing the present value of the large repair cost that can be deferred during the gained period with the cost of the preventive repair gives a rough estimate of the economic value of preventive repair.

ce-19.title: Comprehensive Problem Solving: Cross-Review of a Small Bridge's Structure, Ground, and Drainage
explain: So far we have studied structure, ground, hydraulics and hydrology, and construction and maintenance separately. In real projects, however, they are entangled within a single facility. The reaction of a girder becomes the load on the abutment foundation, and the channel beneath the bridge must carry away the runoff when it rains. This lesson is a practice that links the tools from earlier lessons into one flow, using a single hypothetical small bridge.

The conditions of the hypothetical project 'Mulgilcheon Small Bridge' are as follows. Four simply supported girders with a span of 20 m support the deck, and the load on one girder is assumed to be a uniformly distributed load of 30 kN/m, including self-weight and vehicles. Both abutments stand on a strip foundation 2 m wide and 9 m long, and the self-weight of one abutment is 600 kN. The allowable bearing capacity of the foundation ground is given as 150 kPa. The channel beneath the bridge is a rectangular section that can be used up to 4 m wide and a water depth of 1.5 m, with $n = 0.025$ and $S = 0.001$. The upstream catchment is 0.9 km² with $C = 0.5$, and the rainfall intensity is 80 mm/h.

Review order: ① define the loads; ② find the reactions and maximum moment of the girder (stage 2); ③ gather the load going to the abutment foundation, find the contact pressure, and compare it with the allowable bearing capacity (stage 3); ④ compare the peak runoff of the catchment with the conveyance capacity of the channel (stage 4); ⑤ organize the results, record the assumptions and limits, and add the meaning for construction and maintenance (stage 5).

Structure: the reaction of one girder is $wL/2 = 30 \times 20 / 2 = 300$ kN, and the maximum moment is $wL^2/8$. For a hypothetical girder with a section modulus of 0.075 m³, the maximum bending stress can be found as $M/S$ and compared with a hypothetical allowable value. Ground: one abutment carries the one-side reactions of four girders together with the self-weight of the abutment. Dividing this sum by the foundation area gives the average contact pressure.

Hydraulics: the peak runoff is found by the rational method. For the channel's conveyance capacity, $A = 4 \times 1.5 = 6$ m², $P = 4 + 3 = 7$ m, $R \approx 0.857$ m, and $R^{2/3} \approx 0.902$, so $v = 40 \times 0.902 \times 0.0316 \approx 1.14$ m/s and $Q_{cap} \approx 6.85$ m³/s. Compare the two values to judge whether the channel is sufficient.

Points to note in the overall judgment: passing one item does not mean the whole passes. Every element on the load path and on the water flow path must each satisfy its criterion. Also, the results depend on the assumed loads, coefficients, and rainfall intensity, so one must record which assumption shifts the result most. The project and numbers in this course are all hypothetical for learning and are not actual design judgments.

examples.title: Checking the girder bending stress
body: Condition: one girder with $w = 30$ kN/m, $L = 20$ m, a section modulus of 0.075 m³, and a hypothetical allowable bending stress of 25 MPa.
Step 1: $M_{max} = 30 \times 400 / 8 = 1500$ kN·m.
Step 2: $\sigma = 1500 / 0.075 = 20000$ kN/m² $= 20$ MPa, which is less than the hypothetical allowable value of 25 MPa.
Interpretation: the margin ratio is $25/20 = 1.25$. If the load assumption were more than 25% larger, the criterion would be exceeded, so the basis of the load assumption must be recorded.

examples.title: A framework for comparing channel conveyance with runoff
body: Condition: the conveyance capacity is $Q_{cap} \approx 6.85$ m³/s, and the peak runoff $Q$ is found by the rational method.
Step 1: if $Q \le Q_{cap}$, the channel is considered not to overflow for the given rainfall.
Step 2: if $Q > Q_{cap}$, alternatives are compared, such as enlarging the channel width or depth, or placing a detention basin upstream to lower the peak.

Interpretation: enlarging the channel section changes the abutment locations and the span, so the structure and foundation reviews must be redone. The fact that the disciplines are entangled is the core of the comprehensive review.

checks.prompt: List in order the steps of the integrated review of the small bridge.
checks.hint: The foundation load comes from the girder reactions.
checks.explanation: Load, then girder, then foundation, then drainage, then summary, in that order.
items: Find the reactions and maximum moment of the girder
Find the contact pressure of the abutment foundation and compare it with the allowable bearing capacity
Compare the peak runoff with the channel conveyance capacity
Summarize the results and the assumptions and limits

checks.prompt: What is the maximum bending moment of one girder of Mulgilcheon Small Bridge? (kN·m)
checks.hint: $wL^2/8$, with $w = 30$ kN/m and $L = 20$ m.

checks.prompt: One abutment carries the one-side reactions of 4 girders and the abutment's self-weight of 600 kN. What is the average contact pressure if the foundation is 2 m wide and 9 m long? (kPa)
checks.hint: The reaction of one girder is 300 kN.

checks.prompt: What is the peak runoff by the rational method for the upstream catchment of 0.9 km², with $C = 0.5$ and a rainfall intensity of 80 mm/h? (m³/s)

Which is the correct overall judgment of the results: girder bending stress 20 MPa (hypothetical allowable 25 MPa), foundation contact pressure 100 kPa (allowable 150 kPa), and peak runoff 10 m³/s (conveyance about 6.85 m³/s)?
checks.hint: Compare each item's calculated value with its allowable value, one by one.
checks.explanation: The drainage item exceeds its criterion. If the channel is changed, the spans and foundations must also be reviewed again.
options: Two of the three items pass, so the plan is confirmed as it is
The structure and foundation are within the criteria under the assumed conditions, but the channel conveyance is insufficient, so the channel and span plan must be reviewed again
The foundation contact pressure exceeds the allowable value, so the foundation must be enlarged
The girder stress exceeds the allowable value, so the girder must be replaced

ce-20.title: Academic Capstone: Hypothetical Small Bridge Integrated Review Report
explain: The last lesson is a task of writing a review report yourself. Where the earlier lessons practiced calculating with given numbers, this time you set hypothetical conditions yourself, calculate, and critique how reliable the results are. Judgment in civil engineering gains persuasiveness when it shows not just a single number but its assumptions, basis, and limits together.

The structure of the report is as follows. ① Project overview: the hypothetical location, purpose, span, and width. ② Assumptions: loads, materials, ground coefficients, catchment and rainfall conditions, and the basis of each assumption (state that these are hypothetical values used in this course). ③ Structural review: girder reactions, maximum moment, and bending stress. ④ Ground review: foundation contact pressure and allowable bearing capacity, and, if needed, an estimate of consolidation settlement. ⑤ Hydraulic and hydrologic review: peak runoff and channel conveyance capacity. ⑥ Construction and maintenance memo: the tasks likely to lie on the critical path, the inspection plan, and the parts where deterioration will be fast. ⑦ Critique: the assumptions that most strongly shift the results, alternatives for items that exceed criteria, and what this review does not cover.

The most useful tool in critique is the **sensitivity check**. One key assumption is changed by a fixed percentage (for example ±20%), and the change in the result is observed. Moments are proportional to the load and to the square of the span, so an error in the span assumption shakes the result more than an error in the load assumption. Consolidation settlement is proportional to $C_c$ and responds logarithmically to the stress increase. The runoff is proportional to each of $C$ and $I$. Knowing these relations lets you judge which assumptions must be made more certain.

Results from several disciplines can conflict. Widening a channel improves drainage, but it lengthens the span, increasing the girder moment, and the abutments may move, changing the foundation ground. A good report does not insist on the optimum of one discipline, but compares the pros and cons of alternatives within the same framework. Lifecycle cost and maintenance burden also serve as criteria for comparing alternatives.

Limits: this task is a hypothetical review for learning. Actual bridge design goes through load combinations from design standards, strength reduction factors, seismic and wind reviews, site ground investigation and hydrologic data, and the judgment of qualified experts. The report should state this clearly.

examples.title: Example of a sensitivity check
body: Condition: the girder of Lesson 19 ($w = 30$ kN/m, $L = 20$ m, $M = 1500$ kN·m).
Step 1: if the load increases by 20%, $M = 1800$ kN·m, which is also 20% larger.
Step 2: if the span increases by 20% ($L = 24$ m), $M = 30 \times 576 / 8 = 2160$ kN·m, which is 44% larger.
Interpretation: the span assumption shakes the result more. This is why the basis for the span decision (the channel width) must first be made certain in the report.

examples.title: Example of comparing alternatives
body: Condition: in Lesson 19 the conveyance capacity was insufficient. Alternative (a): widen the channel to 6 m and lengthen the span to 22 m. Alternative (b): place a detention basin upstream to lower the peak runoff.

Step 1: (a) increases the conveyance capacity, but the girder moment becomes $(22/20)^2 \approx 1.21$ times as large, so the bending stress rises to about 24.2 MPa, close to the hypothetical allowable value of 25 MPa.
Step 2: (b) leaves the bridge unchanged but creates a burden of land and maintenance (dredging of sediment).

Interpretation: rather than concluding that one is better, the goal of the capstone is to leave a table and its basis comparing the alternatives on the same criteria (safety margin, cost, maintenance, and environment).

checks.prompt: List in order the sections of the capstone report.
checks.hint: Calculations come after the assumptions, and the critique comes after the calculations.
checks.explanation: Writing in the order overview, assumptions, structure, ground, hydraulics, critique lets the reader follow the load path.

checks.prompt: For the maximum moment of a simply supported girder, which assumption shakes the result most when there is an error of the same ratio (+20%)?
checks.hint: Look at the exponent of each variable in $M = wL^2/8$.
checks.explanation: The span enters squared, so a 20% error in it produces about a 44% change in the moment.
options: Number of girders
Magnitude of the uniformly distributed load
Span length
Self-weight of the abutment

checks.prompt: Summarize in 3 to 5 sentences the overview of the hypothetical small bridge you set, its key assumptions, and the review results for the three fields (structure, ground, and hydraulics).
checks.hint: Shorten each of the sections ① to ⑤ of the report framework to one sentence.
checks.explanation: A summary must show not only the results but also the assumptions that produced them.
checks.model: A hypothetical simple girder bridge with an 18 m span over a river was reviewed. Assuming a uniformly distributed load of 25 kN/m on one girder, the maximum moment is 1012.5 kN·m, and the bending stress in the hypothetical girder section was within the allowable value. The average contact pressure of the abutment foundation was 90 kPa, smaller than the assumed bearing capacity of 150 kPa. The peak runoff of 7 m³/s from the rational method was smaller than the channel conveyance of 8 m³/s from Manning's formula. All values follow from hypothetical assumptions, and the results were most sensitive to the rainfall intensity and span assumptions.
